title: Computing Machinery
body:
COMP 2655 covers what the machine does with a program after the compiler has finished with it.
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] uses a [[Pointer]] and talks about [[Memory]] without
explaining what either one is. This course explains both, by removing the compiler and writing
directly in the instructions the processor executes.

Everything is taught on the [[Motorola 68000]], a real processor from 1979, chosen because its
instruction set is small enough to hold in your head and regular enough that the rules have
few exceptions. [[Assembly]] written here runs on hardware with nothing in between, so a
mistake produces a specific failure the processor can name.

The material continues into [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]], which opens the [[CPU]] and looks at
the logic gates inside, and then into [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]], which takes over at the privilege
boundary this course reaches at the end.

## Topics

### How a computer executes a program

A [[CPU]] repeats one cycle for its entire working life. It fetches the instruction at the
address in the program counter, decodes what that instruction means, executes it, and advances
the program counter to the next instruction. Everything a computer does is that loop.

The 68000 is a [[VonNeumann]] machine, which means instructions and data share one memory and
travel over one [[Bus]]. That is why a program can be loaded like data and then executed, and
why a stray jump into a data area causes the processor to interpret numbers as instructions.
[[Computer Architecture]] covers the arrangement.

The [[CPU]] divides into a control unit that runs the cycle, an [[ALU]] that performs
arithmetic and logic, and registers, which are storage locations inside the processor itself.
Registers are the fastest storage a program can use, and there are very few of them. The 68000
separates them by purpose:

```
d0 - d7    data registers, hold values being worked on
a0 - a7    address registers, hold locations in memory
pc         program counter, address of the next instruction
sr         status register, holds the flags described below
```

[[Main memory]] is much slower than the CPU, which is the reason [[Cache]] exists, and the
[[Clock]] sets the rate at which the fetch and execute cycle advances.

### How numbers and characters are stored

Everything in memory is bits, and a [[Data type]] is an agreement about how to read them.
[[Data representation]] covers the agreements, and [[Base Conversion]] is the working skill,
since the same value is written three ways depending on what is convenient:

```
decimal 42  =  hex $2A  =  binary %00101010

$  hex        @  octal       %  binary       no prefix means decimal
```

Hexadecimal is used constantly because one hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is two
digits and the conversion needs no arithmetic.

[[Integer Representation]] covers signed and unsigned layouts, and [[Complements]] covers two's
complement, which is how negative numbers are stored. Negate a number by inverting every bit
and adding one:

```
  5  =  %00000101
 invert  %11111010
 add 1   %11111011  =  $FB  =  -5 in eight bits
```

The reason for that particular scheme is that it makes subtraction free. Adding $FB to a
number gives the same result as subtracting 5, so one adder circuit performs both operations
and the hardware needs no subtractor.

[[Character Representation]] and [[ASCII]] cover the 7-bit encoding for text, where `'A'` is
65 and `'a'` is 97, so converting case is adding or subtracting 32.
[[Boolean Representation]] covers how a truth value occupies a byte, and
[[Mathematical Operations]] and [[Binary Operations]] cover the arithmetic and bitwise
operators built on these layouts.

### Writing assembly

An assembly program is a list of [[Instructions]], one per line, each translating into one
machine instruction. [[Directives]] sit alongside them and instruct the assembler without
producing any machine code of their own.

```
        move.w  #5,d0        ; put the number 5 into d0
        move.w  #3,d1        ; put the number 3 into d1
        add.w   d1,d0        ; d0 = d0 + d1, so d0 now holds 8
        clr.w   d1           ; d1 = 0
```

Three things are visible there. The operands read source first and destination second, so
`add.w d1,d0` leaves its result in `d0`. The `#` marks a literal value, and its absence means
the operand is an address. The `.w` is a size suffix, and every instruction carries one:

```
.b   byte,      8 bits
.w   word,     16 bits
.l   longword, 32 bits
```

The common directives are `dc` to emit bytes into the program, `ds` to reserve space without
initialising it, and `equ` to name a constant, which emits nothing and substitutes the value
wherever the name appears. An `even` directive after byte data forces the next item onto an
even address, which matters for the reason given under errors below.

### Addressing modes

An [[Addressing Modes|addressing mode]] is how an instruction says where its operand is. The
68000 has four that account for most code:

| Mode | Written | The operand is | C equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Register direct | `d0` | the contents of the register | a local variable |
| Immediate | `#5` | the literal value itself | a constant |
| Absolute | `var` | the value stored at that address | a global variable |
| Register indirect | `(a0)` | the value at the address in `a0` | `*p`, dereferencing |

The last row is the one to understand properly, because it is what a [[Pointer]] is. An
address register holds a location, and the parentheses mean go to that location and use what
is there:

```
        move.l  #list,a0     ; a0 now holds the ADDRESS of list
        move.w  (a0),d0      ; d0 gets the VALUE stored at that address
```

Immediate is never valid as a destination, since writing into a literal has no meaning.

### Arithmetic and the status bits

The [[Status Register]] holds the [[Status Bits]], a handful of flags that describe the result
of the last instruction. Nothing asks for them and almost every instruction sets them, which
is what makes comparison and branching work.

Two of the flags exist because the processor has no idea whether the bits it just added
represent signed or unsigned numbers. Carry reports that an unsigned result was too large for
its size. Overflow reports the same thing for a signed result. The hardware sets both flags on
every operation and the program reads whichever one applies to the interpretation it intends:

```
  200 + 100 in a byte
  unsigned: the true answer is 300, the byte holds 44, carry is set
  signed:   the same bits read as -56 + 100, no signed overflow occurs
```

For `add`, either the source or the destination has to be a data register. `adda` is the
version for address registers, and `ext` sign-extends a value into a larger size, which is how
a negative byte becomes the same negative number in a word.

### Branching and looping

There is no `if` and no `while`. [[Branching and Looping]] builds both from a comparison
followed by a conditional branch.

```
        cmp.w   d1,d0        ; computes d0 - d1 and keeps only the flags
        ble     smaller      ; branch if d0 <= d1
        ...                  ; falls through here when d0 > d1
smaller:
```

`cmp` is a subtraction that discards its result and keeps the flags, and the operand order
reads backwards from the comparison it expresses: `cmp.w d1,d0` compares `d0` against `d1`.
The branch instruction then reads the flags. Signed comparisons use `bgt` and `ble`, unsigned
comparisons use `bhi` and `bls`, and choosing the wrong pair assembles cleanly and returns
wrong answers on values above the signed limit.

`dbra` is the counting loop. It decrements the counter and branches while the counter is above
$-1$, so a loop of $n$ iterations starts its counter at $n-1$:

```
        move.w  #4,d1        ; five iterations
loop:   ...                  ; body
        dbra    d1,loop      ; decrement d1, repeat until it reaches -1
```

### Subroutines and the stack

[[Subroutines]] are functions with the conveniences removed. `jsr` pushes the address of the
next instruction onto the stack and jumps, and `rts` pops that address back into the program
counter and resumes.

```
        jsr     square       ; return address pushed automatically
        ...
square: mulu    d0,d0        ; d0 = d0 * d0
        rts                  ; return address popped, execution resumes
```

The stack grows downwards in memory, `a7` is the stack pointer and is also written `sp`, and
two addressing modes handle it: `-(sp)` decrements then writes, which is a push, and `(sp)+`
reads then increments, which is a pop.

```
        move.l  d0,-(sp)     ; push d0
        ...                  ; use d0 for something else
        move.l  (sp)+,d0     ; pop it back
```

Everything beyond the return address is convention. The processor provides no parameters, no
local variables and no return values, and all three are built by agreeing where on the stack
to put them. That agreement is a calling convention, and it is what makes arguments, locals
and [[Recursion]] possible, since each call pushes its own frame.

### The chips around the processor

A processor alone reaches nothing. Four support chips surround the 68000 and all four return
in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]]. The [[6850 ACIA]] handles the keyboard, converting serial input
into bytes the processor can read. The [[68901 MFP]] is the [[PIC]], the programmable
interrupt controller, deciding which device gets the processor's attention first. The
[[YM2149]] is the [[PSG]] and generates sound. [[GLUE]] is the system controller and
arbitrates access to the bus.

### When a program goes wrong

[[Assembly Errors]] sorts failures by when they occur. Assembly-time errors are syntax and are
caught by the assembler. Link-time errors are unresolved references to labels that were never
defined. Run-time behavioural errors are [[Logic Errors]] and produce no message at all.

Run-time faults crash the program, and the 68000 detects four of them in hardware, each
displaying a different bomb count on screen:

| Fault | Bombs | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| Bus error | 2 | an access outside addressable memory, or to a protected address |
| Address error | 3 | a word or longword access at an odd address |
| Illegal instruction | 4 | executing data as code, usually after a stray jump |
| Privilege violation | 8 | a supervisor-only instruction issued from user mode |

The address error is the one that catches people, and it is why the `even` directive exists.
The 68000 fetches a word from an even address in one bus cycle, and it rejects an odd address
for a word access. Placing an odd number of bytes with `dc` leaves the next item on an odd
address, and the fault appears at the instruction that reads it.
[[Error Detection]] covers detecting corruption in stored and transmitted data.

### Where the operating system starts

The processor has no knowledge of which addresses are protected. It has two modes, user and
supervisor, and certain instructions are legal only in the second. A program running in user
mode that needs a privileged operation asks for it through a [[System Call]], which switches
mode, runs kernel code, and switches back. Attempting the instruction directly raises the
privilege violation above.

That boundary is the last topic of this course and the first of [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]], where
the [[Kernel]] is the code on the privileged side and the [[Operating System]] is what it
provides.

## Related courses

- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) is the direct sequel, opening the [[CPU]] to look at
  [[Digital Logic]], [[Combinational Logic]] and [[Sequential Logic]], and connecting it to
  the world through [[I-O]], [[Interrupts]] and [[Direct Memory Access]].
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] (COMP 3659) builds a full course on [[Kernel]], [[System Call]],
  [[Supervisor State]], [[Main memory]] and [[Cache]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) is the same story in C, where
  [[Memory]], [[Pointer]], [[Stack and Heap]], [[Byte]] and [[Type casting]] are used without
  being explained. This course supplies the mechanism under each one.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] (COMP 2633) uses the same error taxonomy, where
  [[Compile Errors]], [[Logic Errors]] and [[Runtime Errors]] match the split in
  [[Assembly Errors]].
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) supplies the number bases behind [[Base Conversion]] and the
  logic behind [[Boolean Representation]].
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) explains why unsigned overflow is correct behaviour, since
  fixed-width arithmetic is arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$.
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] (COMP 3649) treats [[Assembly]] as the imperative model with
  nothing hidden, and settles the cost of a tail call against the stack discipline in
  [[Subroutines]].
